issues.item: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: The threat items imply a trauma context dominated by interpersonal assault or ambush cues (others' sudden movements, ominous silence) rather than toxic chemical exposure. For a chemical exposure trauma, these are hard to reconcile unless there is additional unreported assault/combat context.

issues.item: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal about losing connection to community/culture is not well anchored to the rest of the profile. The other selected items center on intrusive memory, overwhelm, and coping incapacity, but there are no related triggers, memories, or strategies suggesting social/cultural disconnection as a core post-trauma theme.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: This item is the least coherent with the rest of the profile. For a 72-year-old married male Coast Guard patient with toxic chemical exposure, the dominant pattern elsewhere is threat, intrusive sensory memory, and low coping around reminders. 'Lost connection to my community and culture' is not impossible, but it is not well supported by the trauma type or by the other selected threat/memory/appraisal items, which center on danger, overwhelm, and inability to handle recall. It reads as a broader social-identity consequence that is disconnected from the active formulation, where Memory and Threat are tightly linked and Negative Appraisals are threat-focused. This makes that individual appraisal item clinically weakly matched to the rest of the self-report.

vignette:
Kofi Mensah is a 72-year-old African American man who spent the better part of four decades serving in the United States Coast Guard, retiring as a senior petty officer after a career defined by discipline, physical endurance, and an unshakeable belief that training and vigilance could contain almost any danger the sea might produce. He is married, lives with his wife of forty-one years in a modest home near a coastal station he once served, and until approximately eighteen months ago had considered himself, in his own words, a man who had seen enough to know how to keep himself steady. That self-understanding did not survive what happened in the chemical spill response.

The incident occurred during a routine hazardous materials assist operation when a cargo vessel reported a catastrophic breach in containers holding industrial solvent compounds. Kofi was among the first responders to board. The air on deck was still - unnervingly, completely still - in the way that sometimes precedes a weather event, and he would later recall that the silence itself had felt wrong before anything else did. Within minutes of boarding, his respirator seal failed. He had no way to know how long he breathed the contaminated air before a colleague pulled him back. What he remembered most precisely was the quality of the light, the flat chemical smell that seemed to coat the inside of his throat, the way his eyes burned so sharply that he could not keep them open, and the absolute absence of sound except for his own labored breathing. He was hospitalized for several days, treated for acute respiratory irritation and chemical conjunctivitis, and cleared for return to limited duty within weeks. The medical discharge that followed several months later was attributed to cumulative service-related health considerations, but Kofi privately understood it as connected to that day.

In the months after the incident, something in his relationship to the world shifted in ways he struggled to name. The memories did not fade with time the way he had expected them to. Instead they returned with a fidelity that disturbed him - not as vague impressions but as images so precise and complete they felt less like remembering than like viewing evidence. He would be sitting at his kitchen table and find himself looking at what seemed like a photograph of the deck railing, the particular angle of the containers, the quality of that flat light. At other times the memory ran continuously, scene after scene, and he could not interrupt it. When he tried to sit with it, the emotion that rose was so large and so sudden that he had to physically stand and leave the room, unable to continue whatever he had been doing.

He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt entirely reasonable to him, that thinking about the event directly would undo him - that there was a threshold he would cross from which he would not return intact. So he did not think about it, or tried not to, and organized his days around that effort. He stopped attending the informal gatherings at the station where former colleagues met monthly, because conversations about operations had a way of arriving without warning. His wife noticed that he had become reluctant to leave the house on overcast days, when the flat grey light bore a resemblance he could not explain to her without explaining everything else.

What frightened him most, in a way that surprised even him, was silence. Inside his own home, if his wife left for an errand and the house went quiet, he found himself moving from room to room, checking windows, unable to settle. He was certain that unusual silence meant something was coming, that the absence of sound was not neutral but anticipatory. His body confirmed this: his heart would accelerate, his hands would tighten, his breathing would become shallow in a way that recalled, physically and precisely, the moment the respirator failed.

He had, over eighteen months, become a man who could not tolerate minor disruptions to routine - a delayed phone call, a misplaced set of keys - without a disproportionate response that left him ashamed and exhausted. He had come to believe that the world was genuinely and permanently more dangerous than he had understood it to be, and that he was no longer equipped to navigate it. What finally brought him to the clinic was his wife's quiet observation that she felt she was living with someone who was always waiting for something terrible, and that she was frightened too now. He came hoping, with considerable skepticism, that something might still be retrievable.
